title: Ivy League + Stanford/Duke/UChicago/Georgetown/Northwestern — humanities & social-science admit benchmarks
note: Admit-rate, score, and rank figures are school-wide (CDS does not break out by intended major). topMajors and ecPatterns focus on humanities & social-science fields. No school reports a mean GPA — the CDS records class-rank bands instead. SAT/ACT 50th percentile (p50) is null where the school's CDS reports only 25th/75th. Test policy reflects the current (2025-26) cycle and is in flux at several schools; where a school's most recent CDS cohort predates a policy change, that is noted.

insights: Admit rates for humanities/social-science applicants are governed by the same school-wide numbers shown here — the CDS does not break out admit rate by intended major, so treat these as the realistic baseline regardless of field.

SAT 25th percentiles cluster tightly at 1480-1510 and 75th at 1550-1580 across the Ivies + peers; Georgetown is the clear outlier (25th ~1400, admit ~12.9%) and the most realistic 'reach with strong humanities fit' on this list.

Test policy is in active flux — required now at Harvard, Brown, Dartmouth, Stanford, Georgetown, and Penn (Fall 2026); Cornell all-colleges required Fall 2026; required soon at Yale (Class of 2031) and Princeton (Fall 2028). Columbia (permanent), UChicago, Duke, and Northwestern remain test-optional. Verify the policy for the exact entry year before advising.

No school publishes a mean GPA — they report class-rank bands, and most admits come from a small self-reporting subset (often <30%). Roughly 85-98% of admits who reported rank were in the top tenth; Northwestern reports no GPA/rank at all.

Each school has a signature humanities/social-science draw worth naming in a 'why us' essay: Georgetown SFS (International Relations, #1 in Foreign Policy), Princeton SPIA + graded-paper requirement, Cornell ILR (applied social science), Northwestern Medill (journalism), Duke Sanford (public policy), Penn PPE, Yale EPE, Brown's Open Curriculum.

EC patterns are strikingly consistent: depth-over-breadth 'spikes' in debate/Model UN, mentored or independent research, writing/publication/journalism, and policy or civic engagement — leadership and tangible impact matter more than a long activity list.
